episode_title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone?

stories.topic: ERNET: A Whole Country on 1.54 Megabits
stories.summary: When Ajay first came back to India in the early 1990s, the only internet connectivity in the country was at the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST). Its head, S. Ramani, led a project called ERNET, a single T1 line running at 1.54 megabits per second for all of India. On a tiny budget it seeded hundreds of people with UNIX and internet knowledge, including people the hosts know personally. By the time telecom opened up, that knowledge had already spread across the country.
stories.insight: Small, well-placed investments in knowledge can have huge effects. ERNET built the human capital for the services boom before the bandwidth existed.
stories.quote: So the full country was riding on 1.54 megabits a second.

stories.topic: How Breaking a Monopoly Built India's Biggest Industry
stories.summary: In the late 1990s the Vajpayee government broke the Department of Telecom's stranglehold on telecom policy and opened the sector to private and foreign investment. It also privatised VSNL and ended its monopoly on international telephony. Private firms then laid fibre optic cables into India, with landing stations linking the Middle East to Bombay and Madras to Singapore, until India had effectively infinite bandwidth. Users paid for it, not the government. Ajay's one regret is that this happened in 1999 instead of alongside the early-90s customs duty cuts, which cost India about eight years. Amit recalls the objections of that time: telecom was too important and national security was at stake.
stories.insight: India's cleanest infrastructure success came from the state stepping aside, not from the state spending money. The 'too important to open up' arguments were forgotten once the reform worked.
stories.quote: You don't need government money. You just need user charges that you know, all of us we pay for a broadband line. You don't need government money. This should be about government getting out of the way.

stories.topic: Crawling Up the Coast: Mphasis Finds Cheap Talent
stories.summary: The founder of Mphasis told Ajay how the firm was expanding along the coast of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa. It would pick a town of five to ten lakh people, put up a building, hire 2,000 people and start work. It begins with call centres, where the firm polishes recruits' English accent and grammar, and moves up to software. Workers stay near home instead of migrating, and fibre connects them to global production.
stories.insight: This is the 'equalising differences' theory working as designed. Labour in Vijayawada is cheaper than in Bangalore, so once connectivity exists, work flows to wherever the cheap labour lives.
stories.quote: today we are crawling up the coast of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa. Finding one city after another with a minimum population of five, ten lakh people, and we put a building there, we hire two thousand people there, and we are up and running.

stories.topic: JNPT: Three Competing Terminals in One Port
stories.summary: In the 1990s the government did not hand JNPT to a single private operator. It set the port up as three competing terminals. One stayed with the government so that costs could be measured and prices benchmarked, and the other two were contracted to different private vendors. The result was vigorous competition inside a single port.
stories.insight: Careful policy design can create competition where a monopoly would otherwise form. Ajay notes that this level of design brilliance was rarely repeated in later Indian infrastructure.
stories.quote: Sadly some of that level of brilliance in policy doesn't happen in many later episodes in Indian infrastructure.

stories.summary: Ajay calls himself an enthusiast for India and supported the 1990s infrastructure paradigm. Year after year he watched the goods export data, hoping manufacturing exports would take off as ports, highways, airports and railways were built. For this episode he chose a ten-year window (FY2012-13 to FY2022-23) that deliberately flatters India because it includes the post-pandemic goods boom. Even then, growth was negligible. He openly says his views have shifted.
stories.insight: This is the episode's opening theme in action. The hardest belief to update is one you championed yourself, and measuring honestly over a window chosen to favour your side makes the conclusion hard to dodge.
stories.quote: I just kept watching the data and hoping and watching the data and hoping.

stories.summary: Central planners and optimistic economists in China drove a gigantic infrastructure build. Over time, political decisions led to roads with nothing at the other end. In the short run everyone was happy: there were construction contracts, announcements and ribbon cuttings. Yet each extra unit of investment bought less and less GDP.
stories.insight: By any reasonable account China built too much infrastructure and wasted trillions of dollars of poor people's money. India should ask whether it is heading down a smaller version of the same road.
stories.quote: They started building roads to nowhere and where there was a political decision, they're going to build this road, and there's nothing at the other end. But vast money would be spent.

stories.topic: Two Days Inside a World-Class Jeans Factory
stories.summary: Arvind showed Ajay 'one bad factory and one good factory', and the good one was, by their account, the best blue jeans factory in India. It sits on the outskirts of Bangalore, employs about 2,500 blue-collar workers and exports everything it makes. Because India's minimum wages and mandatory benefits are high, the factory constantly adds machines, each justified by a hard-nosed internal rate of return calculation, to compete with Bangladesh and Vietnam. Even the process of making new jeans look old and faded is now done by robots. The day shift is almost entirely women, while 24-hour operations are 100% men because of safety, transport and regulatory hurdles. Ajay called it one of the greatest two days of his life and asked listeners to suggest more factory visits.
stories.insight: A factory floor shows how India's labour rules shape firms. High mandated labour costs push even labour-intensive industries toward machines that microeconomics calls inefficiently capital-intensive. Amit adds that this hurts the very workers the minimum wage is meant to protect.
stories.quote: In the day shift, it's almost entirely women. But when you get to 24 hour operation, there are all kinds of difficulties on the physical safety, the transportation, on government regulations, and then it's 100% men.

stories.topic: Lonavala Chikki Is Made in Ulhasnagar
stories.summary: Ajay was explaining that you would rather make a product where costs are low and sell it where they are high. Amit asked whether Lonavala chikki was made in China. Ajay said it wasn't, but it was made in Ulhasnagar: he had gone on a field trip to find out. When he asked, the man told him they don't make it in Lonavala, they make it in Ulhasnagar.
stories.insight: A small, memorable example of capitalism equalising differences. Lonavala's real estate is expensive, so production moves somewhere cheaper and the finished product travels back.
stories.quote: But the punchline of the story is the guy answered, Of course we don't make it here. We make it in Ulhasnagar.

recommendations.item: Young Rural Women in India Chase Big-City Dreams
recommendations.creator: Ellen Barry
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the episode: a New York Times piece on young women from Orissa who move to Tirupur to work in low-end garment export factories.
recommendations.reason: Ajay sees firms and exports as the heart and soul of the Indian story. This piece shows the human drama in the lives of the workers behind the export numbers.

recommendations.item: Follow-Up: A New Ending in Tale of Young Woman From Rural India
recommendations.creator: Ellen Barry
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's recommended article, as its sequel.
recommendations.reason: It continues the story of one of the young women from the original Tirupur piece.

recommendations.item: The Odd Woman and the City
recommendations.creator: Vivian Gornick
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, which he framed as 'infrastructure for the mind'. He found the memoir while linking it in the show notes of his Seen and the Unseen episode with Shrayana Bhattacharya.
recommendations.reason: He fell in love with Gornick's writing and says it made him want to write. He gifted the book to Nomsita, they have been reading paragraphs aloud to each other on this trip, and he got Ajay to read a couple of pages too. He calls it a desert island book and 'the best kind of writing which just makes your brain explode'.

recommendations.item: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (Episode 380 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Brought up after Ajay's factory visit, because much of Dhanaraj's work is about women in factories.
recommendations.reason: It is one of Amit's ten favourite episodes. Her parents were factory workers and her mother sold tea for years at a stall on the Coimbatore highway. Amit sees her as the best kind of economist, one who questions received wisdom using real-world experience.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the episode, with Shrayana Bhattacharya, that led Amit to Vivian Gornick.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it is his most popular Seen and the Unseen episode to date.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Education Gone?
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Ajay connects the infrastructure puzzle to the previous episode's education debate, and the paper's title inspires this episode's own title.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett was the child who said the emperor has no clothes. He showed that piling on years of schooling did not deliver development, and Ajay now applies the same scepticism to infrastructure.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit cites 'your great book' while arguing that even infrastructure spending must justify itself.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the argument that every rupee of government spending costs about three rupees of GDP, so public money needs strong reasons.

recommendations.item: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Bastiat while arguing that headline GDP gains from state spending hide its opportunity cost.
recommendations.reason: It is the classic framing for looking past visible spending to what that money could otherwise have done.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned after Ajay explains why politicians prefer ribbon cutting to maintenance.
recommendations.reason: Amit says every Indian absolutely must watch it. It explains that politicians and bureaucrats respond to incentives like everyone else and are not benign institutions.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Amit borrows Graham's phrase 'aggressively conventional-minded' when asking Ajay how to question received beliefs.
recommendations.reason: It names the social pushback anyone faces when they challenge a convenient consensus.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous episode, which Amit and Ajay both use as the template for this one.
recommendations.reason: It re-examines the conventional link between schooling and development, the same kind of assumption-busting this episode applies to infrastructure.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Chess (Episode 52 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's example of a 'synthesis' episode, as opposed to episodes with novel thinking.
recommendations.reason: A synthesis of Amit's knowledge and enthusiasm about chess.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers back to 'when we talked about firms and internationalization' to recall that half or more of global trade is intra-firm.
recommendations.reason: It covers how global firms organise production across countries, which is the basis of the infrastructure theory discussed here.

recommendations.item: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34) and From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37) of Everything is Everything
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit cites the show's episodes on firms as examples of genuinely novel thinking, the category he puts this episode in.
recommendations.reason: They are the show's original thinking on how firms work and evolve.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes next to Ajay's call to walk government contracting through the 'policy pipeline'.
recommendations.reason: It covers how reform actually happens: data, research, rival proposals, public debate, expert committees, laws and implementation.

recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions that his organisation runs a research programme on how governments can contract better.
recommendations.reason: He sees building state capability in government contracting as a high priority now that the state has retreated from PPPs.

core_ideas.concept: Two Barriers to Updating Your Beliefs
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay names two traps. The first is social: conventional wisdom, the mainstream, famous people and Nobel laureates. He says he has resisted this since childhood by treating great thinkers as the kick-off for an argument rather than an authority. The second is arrogance, which he finds harder: refusing to revise conclusions you worked hard to reach. He admits he changes his mind too slowly, and that we are all less Bayesian than we should be.
core_ideas.quote: The second trap is arrogance. The second trap is oh I figured it out, I thought about it, I'll refuse to change my mind.

core_ideas.explanation: Cutting customs duties makes imported raw materials and inputs cheaper, so Indian exports become more competitive. The 1990s tariff cuts produced an export surge. The common belief that a country needs more protectionism to export is backwards.
core_ideas.quote: every bad economist thinks that if India wants to export, you need to do more protectionism. That's just trivially and factually wrong.

core_ideas.concept: Development Means Hosting Global Value Chains
core_ideas.explanation: Half or more of global trade happens inside firms. Multinationals place each stage of production wherever it is cheapest: a ball bearing goes to Brazil, an engine is made there, and the car is assembled in Madras. A country prospers by becoming host to these production chains, whether the firms are Indian or foreign. That requires moving intermediate goods cheaply to remote low-wage places, which is why infrastructure was given top priority in Indian development strategy.
core_ideas.quote: We have no interest in nationality. We just care that production should be done in India.

core_ideas.explanation: Any gap in wages, land or raw material costs is a business opportunity: produce where it is cheap and sell where prices are high. Low-end garment work does not belong in Bombay. The chikki sold in Lonavala gets made in Ulhasnagar. Looking for such differences is a simple trick for understanding where economic activity goes.
core_ideas.quote: Capitalism works by equalizing differences. So if there's a difference in a wage there's a business opportunity

core_ideas.concept: Foreign Firms Seed Domestic Industries Through Their Alumni
core_ideas.explanation: Foreign firms often lead because they already have global production systems and customer relationships. People who worked in them then leave to start domestic firms. Bangladesh's garment industry grew this way from a few pioneers, and Indian software grew from early firms like Datamatics and TCS. This is one reason FDI matters beyond the capital it brings.
core_ideas.quote: very often what works is that the foreign firms lead the way, they come and establish the early facilities, and then the alumni of these firms turn around and build the Indian firms.

core_ideas.concept: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? Services Yes, Goods No
core_ideas.explanation: Telecom infrastructure delivered a services revolution: IT-ITES is now India's biggest industry, with roughly $300-400 billion a year of fast-growing exports. Ports, highways, airports and railways were meant to do the same for goods, and they did not. From FY2012-13 to FY2022-23, a window that flatters India, goods exports grew about 4% a year in nominal dollars and about 1.3% in real dollars, which means doubling only every half-century or so. FDI grew about 4% a year in real terms. Ajay insists on measuring in constant US dollars so exchange rates and inflation cannot create a money illusion. Global firms have not chosen India as a manufacturing platform.
core_ideas.quote: IT today is India's biggest industry. IT is what India does. IT is the only thing India has won in.

core_ideas.concept: ICOR: Why Infrastructure Gives Less Bang for the Buck
core_ideas.explanation: The incremental capital output ratio (ICOR) compares extra capital invested with the extra output it produces. Ajay gives four reasons it has worsened for Indian infrastructure. First, diminishing returns: the best projects, such as the Golden Quadrilateral, JNPT and the Delhi metro, get done first, and a metro in Nagpur costs about as much but is worth far less. Second, the shift from PPPs to government projects, which cost more and are maintained worse. Third, project choice becomes political, favouring powerful constituencies, religious sites or swing seats. Fourth, public choice incentives favour launching projects over running them.
core_ideas.quote: The best projects get taken up early. And then later on, the next wave of projects that are done will always have a lower bang for the buck.

core_ideas.concept: The Hard Part of Being a State Is the Humdrum Part
core_ideas.explanation: Politicians and civil servants enjoy announcements, contracts and inaugurations. The unglamorous work of operating assets, regulating private players and overseeing projects wins no applause, and this is where the Indian state is weakest. Weak infrastructure regulation and poorly run airports are the result.
core_ideas.quote: So the challenge of being a state is the challenge of high quality, quiet humdrum work where you don't get applause and you don't score propaganda points.

core_ideas.concept: Contracting Is a Core State Capability
core_ideas.explanation: From 1991 to 2011, India made a heroic attempt at public-private partnership (PPP) infrastructure. Many contracts went badly because the state's contracting skills were poor. The right response was to research those failures and improve step by step. Instead the government retreated to building things itself, which costs more and maintains worse. Ajay argues states should do complex contracts with private players in defence, innovation, vaccines and infrastructure rather than build. Amit draws the wider lesson: don't run from hard problems just because they're hard.
core_ideas.quote: the right solution is not for a government to build stuff, but for a government to do complex contracts with private persons and get things done from the society

core_ideas.concept: Viability Gap Funding: Subsidise Externalities Without Losing Discipline
core_ideas.explanation: In a PPP, private investors check the traffic projections before committing money, so roads to nowhere get filtered out. Some roads also bring wider benefits that tolls alone can't capture. Ashok Lahiri's idea at the Ministry of Finance was viability gap funding: the government specifies the road, bidders compete in a reverse auction on how little subsidy they need, and the subsidy is then fixed. The private builder keeps the incentive to build well and maintain the asset.
core_ideas.quote: So you get this automatic sanity check in private led projects.

core_ideas.concept: Find the Binding Constraint Before You Spend
core_ideas.explanation: The central question in development economics is what most holds back firms, Indian or foreign, from producing across India. Infrastructure is probably not that choke point today. Ajay offers capital controls or hostile taxation as a hypothetical alternative. If fixing those brought a surge of FDI, jammed ports and roads would make infrastructure the constraint again. As with education, stop putting public money into what isn't working until you have diagnosed why.
core_ideas.quote: And infrastructure is probably not the binding constraint today.

core_ideas.concept: The Unseen Cost of Public Spending
core_ideas.explanation: Each rupee the government spends costs the economy about three rupees, and the coercion of taxation carries a moral cost as well. GDP counts state spending as output whether or not it creates value, so pointless work still raises GDP. Bastiat's lesson is to ask what the money would have done if left with the taxpayers it was taken from.
core_ideas.quote: you could just have an army of people digging up ditches, filling them up, digging up ditches, filling them up, rinse and repeat and the GDP just keeps going up.

core_ideas.concept: Minimum Wages Push Firms Toward Machines
core_ideas.explanation: High minimum wages and mandatory benefits push Indian factories into inefficient capital intensity, replacing workers with machines one investment at a time to compete with Bangladesh and Vietnam. Amit puts it bluntly: anyone whose work is valued below the legal minimum is not paid more. They lose the job.
core_ideas.quote: So instead of earning X amount, they're earning zero, and everybody would agree that zero is worse.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens by noting that Ajay is wearing a sparkling white kurta ('the Sanskari look') with an ant climbing up his collar. Later he interrupts Ajay's account of being a lifelong free thinker to report that the ant is now on his neck, then says: 'Anyway, continue.'
Ajay says the Lonavala chikki is made in Ulhasnagar. Amit: 'So you could actually write on it made in USA. USA standing for Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.'
Ajay mocking the old schooling paradigm: 'if only India will develop years of schooling comparable to the UK of 1947, then India will become like the UK of 1947.'
Ajay on diminishing returns: a Delhi metro is valuable, but 'by the time you're doing a metro in Nagpur, you know, frankly, there's very little use of a metro in Nagpur.'

After describing infrastructure climbing onto the 'high table of development strategy' and declaring itself top priority, Ajay catches himself: 'Now I'm anthropomorphizing a block named infrastructure.'
John Maynard Keynes: 'When the facts change, I change my mind, and what do you do, sir?' Ajay holds this up as the ideal and admits he changes his mind too slowly.

Ajay lists the economists he admires but argues with: Larry Summers, Marty Feldstein, Lant Pritchett and Jeff Hammer. He treats them as a kick-off for an argument: 'Puny little me is going to argue about this with a great person.'
Paul Graham's phrase 'aggressively conventional-minded', from The Four Quadrants of Conformism, which Amit uses for the people who push back on anyone questioning a consensus.

The Emperor's New Clothes: Ajay casts Lant Pritchett as 'the little child saying that the emperor has no clothes' with his paper 'Where Has All the Education Gone?', which gives this episode its title.
Frédéric Bastiat and 'the seen and the unseen': Amit invokes Bastiat to argue that state spending hides a large opportunity cost.
